entries.title: Making working memory work: a meta-analysis of executive-control and working memory training in older adults

outcomes.note: Significant trained-task and near-transfer net gains versus active and passive controls; 49 articles, 61 samples
Far transfer smaller than near; significant for net pretest-posttest gain vs passive and net posttest vs active and passive

findings: No difference between adaptive and nonadaptive training
Gains did not vary with total training time
Training effects in older adults did not differ from younger adults
limitations: Effect magnitudes not given in the abstract
entries.product_use: Backs near-transfer-first claims and the choice not to market adaptivity as a superior mechanism in older adults.

entries.title: Working memory training in typically developing children: A multilevel meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Small-to-medium memory-task effects, proportional to training-outcome similarity; k=393 effect sizes
Active-control far-transfer subgroup: g=0.001, SE=0.055, p=.982, tau2=0.000
Mathematics and language achievement essentially unaffected

findings: Near transfer scales with task similarity, not with general capacity
Null or low true heterogeneity once control type and artifacts are modelled
limitations: Effect magnitudes for near transfer given qualitatively in the abstract
entries.product_use: Do not claim intelligence or school-attainment gains from WM training in children; near-transfer wording only.

entries.title: Anxiety-reducing effects of working memory training: A systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Post-training anxiety reduced, p=.009; negative value = symptom reduction; no CI in abstract

findings: Subgroup effects of anxiety type, anxiety measure and training environment were significant
19 randomised trials from 477 records; low-to-moderate risk of bias
limitations: Heterogeneous training paradigms and anxiety measures
Comparator type not specified beyond 'control condition' in the abstract
entries.product_use: Context only: a small anxiety signal exists but Noesis makes no treatment claim; route distress to support resources.

entries.title: A Systematic Review on Predictors of Working Memory Training Responsiveness in Healthy Older Adults: Methodological Challenges and Future Directions

outcomes.note: 16 studies, 675 adults aged 55+; age, education, intelligence and baseline WM most studied; no clear conclusions

findings: Five prognostic-model and 18 single-factor approaches reported, often with conflicting results
Attrition, confounding and statistical reporting information missing in many studies
entries.product_use: Do not personalise training dose or task assignment by baseline profile; no validated predictor exists.

entries.title: Working memory updating training promotes plasticity & behavioural gains: A systematic review & meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Large training effect and moderate same-domain near transfer; magnitudes not in abstract
Far transfer to other cognitive domains non-significant
Consistent frontoparietal activity decreases; subcortical changes both up and down

findings: Behavioural gains and frontoparietal plasticity co-occur after updating training
Generalisation beyond the trained domain remains unsupported
limitations: No pooled numeric estimates in the abstract
entries.product_use: Supports mechanism-and-measurement framing; do not show neural change as proof of everyday benefit.

entries.title: Benefits of a working memory training program for inattention in daily life: a systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Inattention in daily life; 13 comparisons; negative = fewer symptoms
Follow-up in 7 studies
Visuospatial WM
Verbal WM

findings: Effect present in children and adults, with and without ADHD, and against active and passive controls
One author had previously consulted for Cogmed (declared)
limitations: 2 of 7 follow-up studies drive the persistence estimate
entries.product_use: Supports a narrow daily-inattention near-transfer statement for one named programme, not a general Noesis claim.

entries.title: A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence on the near- and far-transfer effects among children's executive function skills

outcomes.note: Near transfer to the trained component, k=43, p<.001
Far transfer to untrained components, k=17, p=.11; not convincing

findings: Training a component does not significantly improve untrained executive components
Helps explain absent WM-training transfer to academic skills
limitations: Comparator detail not reported in the abstract
entries.product_use: Reinforces training-the-component, measure-the-component product rule and forbids cross-component transfer claims.

entries.title: Visual search training benefits from the integrative effect of enhanced covert attention and optimized overt eye movements

outcomes.note: Conjunction-search training improved search behaviour, reduced saccade count and total scan time; no pooled effect size in abstract
Larger N2pc to the trained target; neural mechanism, not an everyday benefit

findings: Training improved conjunction search and produced larger, more efficient scanning
N2pc results were read as enhanced covert attention to the trained target
limitations: No pooled effect estimate reported in the abstract
Laboratory conjunction-search protocol, not the shipped app task
entries.product_use: Grounds the experimental conjunction-search focus test and its task-practice-only claim; no general attention benefit is claimed.

entries.title: Effects of engagement, persistence and adherence on cognitive training outcomes in older adults with and without cognitive impairment: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials

outcomes.note: Cross-domain effect over 55 RCTs; mean age 73.9 years; normal cognition, MCI and dementia pooled
Effects significant when engagement or persistence exceeded 60% or adherence exceeded 80%; subgroup moderator, not a causal threshold

findings: Higher persistence was needed for memory, visuospatial and reasoning gains than for executive function, attention and language
Older adults with normal cognition required higher persistence for gains than those with impairment
limitations: Subgroup thresholds are observational moderators, not dose targets
Heterogeneous cognitive conditions pooled across normal cognition, MCI and dementia
entries.product_use: Grounds an evidence-linked adherence note: trial benefits appeared above study-level engagement/adherence thresholds, which are context and not a personal target or guarantee.

entries.title: The impact of cognitive training and mental stimulation on cognitive and everyday functioning of healthy older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Versus active controls: working memory p=0.04, processing speed p<0.0001, composite cognition p=0.001; 31 RCTs, 1806 training plus 386 mental-stimulation participants
Versus no intervention: face-name recall p=0.02, immediate recall p=0.02, paired associates p=0.001
Impact on everyday functioning largely under-investigated; no pooled estimate reported

findings: Transfer and maintenance were most commonly reported with adaptive training, at least ten sessions and long-term follow-up
Everyday-function effects remain under-studied in cognitively healthy older adults
limitations: P values reported instead of effect sizes in the abstract
General mental stimulation evidence remains limited
entries.product_use: Grounds the result-view note that everyday-function transfer is not established; trained-task and near-transfer gains are the defensible claim.

entries.title: Everyday Impact of Cognitive Interventions in Mild Cognitive Impairment: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

outcomes.note: Small significant median effect on activities of daily living; 30 controlled studies in MCI
Mood median effect; computerized studies benefited mood most
Metacognitive outcomes median effect
Quality of life not significant

findings: Therapist-based and multimodal interventions affected ADLs and metacognition more than controls; computerized studies mainly helped mood
Everyday generalization in MCI is encouraging but small and limited by database and language restrictions
limitations: Only MEDLINE and PsycINFO searched; published data only
entries.product_use: Context for the claim boundary: small everyday effects appear in MCI interventions, but they are not a basis for an app claim in healthy users.

entries.title: Computerized cognitive training in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials with blinded and objective outcomes

outcomes.note: Probably-blinded ADHD total and hyperactivity/impulsivity post-treatment; abstract prints intervals with reversed signs, so CI omitted and magnitude retained
Small inattention effect; doubled in the intervention delivery setting (SMD 0.40, 0.09-0.71), suggesting setting specificity
Verbal working memory, 15 trials
Visuospatial working memory, 9 trials
No effect on reading or arithmetic outcomes

findings: 36 RCTs, 17 on working-memory training; no probably-blinded effect on total or hyperactivity symptoms
Working-memory gains were short-term; longer-term verbal WM, reading comprehension and executive-function ratings rest on 5-7 trials
limitations: Clinical ADHD population, not the app's audience
entries.product_use: Grounds the app's no-ADHD-treatment claim: blinded outcomes show no clinical symptom effect, only task-near working-memory gains.

entries.title: Game-based brain training for improving cognitive function in community-dwelling older adults: A systematic review and meta-regression

outcomes.note: Game-based training versus control, 15 RCTs, 759 community-dwelling older adults
Selective attention
Short-term memory
Preferable design features: non-time-pressure games, multiplayer, computer platform, provider support, sessions <=3/week and <=60 min; game design moderated processing speed (beta=0.211, p=0.008)

findings: Small near-domain gains in processing speed, selective attention and short-term memory
Meta-regression linked game design to processing-speed effects; no publication bias detected
limitations: Subgroup design preferences are observational, not a dose prescription
Confidence intervals not printed in the abstract
entries.product_use: Grounds the clock-option note: non-time-pressure formats were among preferable features in the older-adult game-training literature, as group-level context rather than a personal rule.

entries.title: Does the combination of exercise and cognitive training improve working memory in older adults? A systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Combined exercise and cognitive training versus no intervention, 21 RCTs
Combined training versus exercise alone; not significant
Combined training versus cognitive training alone; not significant

findings: Combined training beats no intervention on working memory but not either component alone
Effects were moderated by intervention frequency and baseline cognitive state
limitations: No evidence of synergy over single components
entries.product_use: Grounds the no-synergy claim boundary: combined programmes can help versus no intervention, but adding exercise to cognitive training has not shown a reliable extra working-memory benefit.

entries.journal: Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease
entries.title: Expectancy Does Not Predict 18-month Treatment Outcomes with Cognitive Training in Mild Cognitive Impairment

outcomes.note: Baseline expectancy not associated with change in global cognition, everyday function or hippocampus volume to week 78; no expectancy-by-treatment interaction
Participants expected more benefit from computerized training than from crossword puzzles; lower expectancy related to older age and lower baseline global cognition

findings: Expectancy ratings were higher for computerized training than for the crossword control
Expectancy did not predict 78-week response and did not modify treatment effect
limitations: Single two-site RCT, not a pooled estimate
entries.product_use: Context for the expectancy boundary: baseline optimism is not a validated responder predictor, so the app does not personalise assignment by self-expectancy.

entries.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Cognitive Training in Adults with Major Depressive Disorder

outcomes.note: Moderate pooled cognitive and affective effects after cognitive training in diagnosed MDD; magnitudes not printed in abstract
Affective outcomes improved in the clinical MDD sample; not a consumer-app or healthy-user result
Very few studies examined far transfer to everyday functioning

findings: Nine controlled studies from 448 identified; heterogeneous but moderate pooled effects
Everyday-function transfer rarely measured
entries.product_use: Context for the mood-treatment boundary: clinical affective effects in diagnosed MDD do not license a consumer-app treatment or wellbeing claim.

entries.title: Serious Games for Learning Among Older Adults With Cognitive Impairment: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 5 of 11 RCTs: serious games improved verbal learning versus no/sham (P=.04); equal to conventional exercise (2 RCTs, P=.98)
4 of 11 RCTs versus no/sham (P=.03) and 2 versus conventional cognitive training (P<.001) for nonverbal learning

findings: Serious games improved verbal and nonverbal learning in impaired older adults, but meta-analyses used only 2-5 of 11 trials
Authors conclude games should supplement, not replace, established interventions
limitations: Small samples in 6 of 8 pooled studies
entries.product_use: Context for the game rationale: serious-game learning effects in impaired older adults are low-certainty, so Noesis games are task practice and never a replacement for care.

entries.title: The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship

outcomes.note: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable principles for scholarly data; a guideline, not an effect estimate

findings: FAIR principles emphasise machine-readable metadata and explicit reuse conditions
limitations: Consensus principles, not empirical outcome evidence
entries.product_use: Grounds the research export manifest and data dictionary: local CSV/JSON exports carry field documentation and explicit consent metadata.

entries.title: How do we measure data sharing in the biomedical sciences? A measurement systematic review of biomedical data sharing-related knowledge, attitudes and practices across stakeholder groups, data types and geographies

outcomes.note: 60 surveys from 72 publications; fewer than one-third pilot tested, only 3 reported measurement properties, indicating low certainty in data-sharing attitude measurement

findings: Data-sharing KAP surveys are heterogeneous and weakly validated
limitations: Most surveys used once and from high-income settings
entries.product_use: Context for consent design: data-sharing attitudes are not measured reliably, so Noesis uses explicit, revocable consent rather than inferred willingness.

entries.title: Does Far Transfer Exist? Negative Evidence From Chess, Music, and Working Memory Training

outcomes.note: Three meta-analyses (chess, music, working-memory training) found small-to-moderate effects inversely related to design quality; far transfer rarely observed

findings: Effect sizes shrink as experimental quality rises, notably with active controls
Chess, music and working-memory training all fail to show robust far transfer
limitations: No pooled estimate printed in abstract
entries.product_use: Grounds the Evidence screen's near-versus-far gradient: the app reports near transfer and treats far transfer as a research question.

entries.title: Efficacy of memory training interventions targeting metacognition for older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Metacognitive training on memory; 25 studies, 1768 older adults
Metacognitive beliefs; strategic training d=0.48 (0.28-0.69)

findings: Strategy use improved most (d=0.98 metacognitive, d=0.87 strategic)
Methodological quality of most studies was limited; well-designed confirmation needed
limitations: Training protocols are structured interventions, not a single reflection prompt
entries.product_use: Grounds the confidence-check caveat: structured metacognitive training shows benefits in trials but with limited study quality; the app's prompt is reflection, not that intervention.

entries.title: Enhancing reading accuracy through visual search training using symbols

outcomes.note: Reading accuracy improved in the session after a month of daily symbol-search game training, without a speed-accuracy trade-off; correlated with time spent training

findings: Symbol search practice transferred to reading accuracy in 21 children with reading disorders
limitations: Training periods introduced within-subject, no parallel control group
entries.product_use: Context for Visual Search: a clinical single-group study of symbol search shows a reading-accuracy signal, but it is not a basis for an academic or general-attention claim.

entries.title: A meta-analysis and systematic review of reactivity to judgements of learning

outcomes.note: Overall JOL reactivity is not significant; the app's block-level prompt is descriptive
Related word pairs; word lists g=0.384 (0.146-0.622); no reactivity for unrelated or mixed pairs

findings: Eliciting judgements of learning does not reliably change memory overall
Reactivity depends on material: related pairs and word lists show moderate effects, unrelated pairs none
limitations: Item-level judgements, not a block-level reflection prompt
entries.product_use: Grounds the briefing confidence caveat: JOL reactivity is near zero overall and material-dependent, so the app's reflection prompt is not presented as a memory intervention.

entries.title: The role of motivation factors in exergame interventions for fall prevention in older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Motivation and capability components influence exergame outcomes; exergames promising versus traditional exercise but may not improve fall risk or cognitive performance

findings: COM-B motivation and capability components influence intervention outcome
Exergame training alone may not improve fall risk or cognitive performance
entries.product_use: Context for Motivation mode: motivation supports adherence processes, but a game format alone does not establish cognitive or safety outcomes; rewards stay cosmetic.

entries.title: A game-factors approach to cognitive benefits from video-game training: A meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 63 studies, 118 investigations, N=2079; overall cognitive gain g=0.25 (p<.001)
Transfer to attention/perception and higher-order cognition; gameplay features, not genre labels ('action', 'strategy', 'casual'), predicted outcomes

findings: Small overall cognitive benefit from video-game training
Genre labels are not predictive; individual gameplay features are
limitations: No confidence interval printed in abstract
entries.product_use: Context for the game mechanics: small overall effects and feature-level (not genre-level) prediction justify claim-bounded games rather than genre-based promises.

entries.title: Effects of spatial training on mathematics performance: A meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 29 controlled studies, N=3765, k=89; math transfer g=0.28 (SE=0.07), larger for near outcomes
Spatial thinking improved g=0.49 (SE=0.09); concrete manipulatives outperformed computerized training

findings: Spatial training improves spatial thinking and yields smaller math transfer
Concrete materials beat computerized paradigms; near transfer exceeds distal transfer
limitations: Computerized training was the weaker paradigm
entries.product_use: Context for Mental Rotation: a screen-based spatial game can practice spatial thinking but has no academic claim, especially given weaker computerized effects.

entries.title: Meta-analysis of action video game impact on perceptual, attentional, and cognitive skills

outcomes.note: Long-term intervention studies versus other commercial game genres; cross-sectional player difference g=0.55
Top-down attention and spatial cognition most robustly enhanced; perception encouraging

findings: Intervention effects (g=0.34) are smaller than habitual-player differences (g=0.55)
Publication bias estimated to inflate published effects by about 30 percent
limitations: Action-game genre excluded from Noesis on safety grounds
entries.product_use: Context for the game-format boundary: action games show small causal effects with substantial bias, and are excluded from Noesis for flashing/fast-presentation safety reasons.

entries.title: The effectiveness of Go/No-Go and Stop-Signal training in reducing food consumption and choice: A systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Small reduction in food consumption/choice after Go/No-Go or Stop-Signal training with food cues; single-session Go/No-Go g=-0.31 (-0.45,-0.18)

findings: Small effect on food-related behaviour, not on cognitive transfer
Go/No-Go effect robust across moderators; stop-signal parameters varied
entries.product_use: Context for Go/No-Go: the inhibition literature outside cognitive training targets appetitive behaviour, so the app does not claim Stop-Signal or eating-behaviour benefits.

entries.title: Resting-state fMRI detects the effects of learning in short term: A visual search training study

outcomes.note: Trained group showed enhanced resting-state connectivity in visual-search regions after 30 minutes of training; whole-brain networks unchanged
Connectivity change tracked individual learning; no everyday-function outcome

findings: Short-term training altered task-relevant resting connectivity
No whole-network change; neural mechanism only
entries.product_use: Context for Visual Search: neural adaptation after short training is a mechanism finding, not evidence of cognitive or everyday benefit.

entries.title: Investigating Rewards and Deposit Contract Financial Incentives for Physical Activity Behavior Change Using a Smartphone App: Randomized Controlled Trial

outcomes.note: Incentive arms 13.10 days vs control 8.00 days achieved (P=.002); deposit 14.88 vs reward 12.13 not significant (P=.17)
Deposit-contract uptake 62% versus reward 100%; loss frames 10.50 days vs gain frames 14.67 (P=.007), favouring gain framing

findings: Financial incentives beat no incentive, but deposit contracts were not superior and had lower uptake
Loss framing was less effective than gain framing
entries.product_use: Grounds Motivation mode's cosmetic-only rewards and gain framing: real stakes reduced uptake, loss framing underperformed, and Noesis uses no money or loss frames.

entries.title: Persuasive Technology and computational manipulation: hypernudging out of mental self-determination

outcomes.note: Unperceived AI persuasion via dark patterns can undermine autonomy and mental self-determination; no empirical effect estimate

findings: Computational manipulation targets automatic processes without awareness
Autonomy and informational self-determination are the affected rights
limitations: Conceptual legal paper, not an empirical trial
entries.product_use: Grounds Noesis's autonomy posture: no push channel, no hidden incentives, and conspicuous cosmetic rewards that the user can switch off.

entries.title: Influence of reward motivation on human declarative memory

outcomes.note: Reward value can prioritise encoding and consolidation and generalise to related items, altering memory structure; no pooled estimate

findings: Reward guides attention and memory consolidation
Learned reward values can generalise to related representations
limitations: Reward paradigms are not app momentum
entries.product_use: Context for Motivation mode: cosmetic rewards can still bias what is learned, so they never change scores, content or claims.

entries.title: Computer-Based Executive Function Training for Combat Veterans With PTSD: A Pilot Clinical Trial Assessing Feasibility and Predictors of Dropout

outcomes.note: Home-based training dropout 38.5% (executive function) and 57.1% (word-game placebo) over six weeks; completers reported liking the programme
Improved on trained tasks but not traditional neuropsychological assessments

findings: Dropout is common in home-based training even in supervised trials
Trained-task gains did not generalise to standard tests
entries.product_use: Context for the adherence card: early endings are common and non-judgemental logging is appropriate; the app makes no treatment claim.

entries.title: A meta-analysis of perceptual and cognitive functions involved in useful-field-of-view test performance

outcomes.note: 116 correlations from 18 articles; every domain correlated with every UFOV subtest and no subtest was selectively sensitive to one domain

findings: UFOV scores show high ecological validity but none of the three subtests measures one clear construct
A range of visual and cognitive functions contributes to each subtest
limitations: UFOV is proprietary and brief by design
entries.product_use: Grounds the choice of single-construct focus tests: a composite score would hide which function changed, so Noesis reports block-level measures separately.

entries.title: Building the foundations for global data banking in digital phenotyping for mental health

outcomes.note: Priorities: harmonised data standards, hybrid broad-plus-dynamic consent, governance co-designed with lived experience, privacy-preserving reuse

findings: Hybrid consent models preserve participant control as analytics evolve
Standardisation and co-designed governance are prerequisites for trustworthy reuse
entries.product_use: Context for research export: Noesis uses a versioned, revocable consent and a documented field dictionary so participation stays controllable and data stay interpretable.

entries.title: Good Learners Are Poor Monitors: A Negative Relation Between Learning Ability and Monitoring Accuracy

outcomes.note: Meta-analysis N=2406 found slightly poorer JOL monitoring resolution among stronger learners; two controlled replications supported the negative association

findings: Learning ability and monitoring accuracy were negatively related
Expert learners showed underconfidence for items they later recalled
limitations: JOL resolution is a group-level index, not an individual diagnostic
No pooled effect size in abstract
entries.product_use: Context for the confidence note: monitoring accuracy is not a reliable self-diagnostic even for strong learners, so the app's prompt stays descriptive.

entries.title: Systematic review and meta-analyses of useful field of view cognitive training

outcomes.note: 44 studies from 17 RCTs: UFOV training enhanced speed of processing, attention and neural outcomes; effects equivalent against active and no-contact controls
Far transfer to everyday function and well-being reported, with gains enduring up to ten years; no transfer to other neuropsychological outcomes

findings: Functional transfer and long-term durability reported for proprietary UFOV training
Adaptive and community-based protocols produced larger effects
limitations: UFOV is a proprietary, brief composite protocol
Some trials had financial interests; construct purity is doubtful (PMID 29270605)
entries.product_use: Context for Visual Search: UFOV has ecological evidence but is proprietary and not construct-pure, so Noesis uses transparent single-construct focus tests instead.

entries.title: Integrating psychological and neurobiological considerations regarding the development and maintenance of specific Internet-use disorders: An Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model

outcomes.note: I-PACE process model: predisposing factors, coping styles and cognitive biases interact with affective responses and reduced executive control to maintain excessive use

findings: Cue-reactivity and reduced executive control are proposed maintenance mechanisms
Model hypotheses still require empirical testing
limitations: Theoretical model, not an intervention trial
entries.product_use: Context for Motivation safeguards: Noesis avoids variable-ratio stakes, losing and push cues because those are the cue-reactivity routes the model identifies.

entries.title: A Game a Day Keeps Cognitive Decline Away? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Commercially-Available Brain Training Programs in Healthy and Cognitively Impaired Older Adults

outcomes.note: 43 studies, 2636 participants across seven commercial programs; small significant near-transfer effects in healthy and MCI samples

Far transfer absent in MCI; small subjective-only effect in healthy adults. After publication-bias adjustment only processing speed remained significant; no transfer to attention, everyday function, Gf or visuospatial

findings: Commercial programs show near transfer but no robust general or everyday benefit
Publication-bias adjustment removed most domain effects
entries.product_use: Grounds the no-general-gain boundary: the app offers enjoyment and task practice only, with no memory, intelligence or everyday-function claim.

entries.title: Effectiveness of cognitive-motor dual task training in preventing falls in community older adults: A meta-analysis and systematic review

outcomes.note: Dual-task training improved gait, static/dynamic balance (>=12 weeks) and executive function and reduced fall risk versus traditional fall prevention
Effects on lower-limb strength and fear of falling remained controversial

findings: Motor+cognitive dual-task training improves balance, gait and executive function
Long-term effectiveness needs higher-quality trials
limitations: Requires physical movement, absent from Noesis
entries.product_use: Context for the modality boundary: Noesis is screen-based with no motor component, so it makes no gait, balance or fall-prevention claim.

entries.title: Comparative effectiveness of different dual task mode interventions on cognitive function in older adults with mild cognitive impairment or dementia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis

outcomes.note: Dual cognitive task training ranked best for global cognition (SUCRA 79.2%); motor-cognitive dual task was the only mode improving executive function (SMD 1.53, 95% CI 0.06-3.01)
Motor-cognitive dual task also improved activities of daily living (SMD 1.50) and quality of life (1.20)

findings: Dual cognitive task training ranked highest for global cognition
Motor-cognitive modes improved executive function and daily function in MCI/dementia
limitations: Wide confidence intervals on executive-function estimate
entries.product_use: Context for the modality boundary: dual-task cognitive gains are clinical-population, movement-based findings, not a claim for a screen-based consumer tool.

entries.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
entries.title: Placebo effects in cognitive training

outcomes.note: Suggestive recruitment produced apparent fluid-intelligence gains after one hour of training (equivalent to 5-10 IQ points); nonsuggestive controls showed none

findings: Placebo expectancy can mimic large cognitive-training gains
Expectancy confounds can explain industry-style claims
limitations: Young-adult sample and suggestive recruitment paradigm
entries.product_use: Grounds the no-intelligence-gain boundary and the neutral claim language: suggestive framing can manufacture apparent gains, so the app avoids such promises.

entries.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
entries.title: Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals

outcomes.note: Forming specific plans for unfulfilled goals removed intrusive thoughts and freed cognitive resources; several lab studies

findings: Specific plans reduce goal-related intrusion
Effect mediated by earnestness of the plan
entries.product_use: Grounds the optional when-and-where practice plan: making a concrete plan reduces the mental load of an unfulfilled intention.

entries.title: Losses disguised as wins in modern multi-line video slot machines

outcomes.note: 40 novices: wins and losses-disguised-as-wins produced similarly elevated arousal, both above ordinary losses

findings: Reinforcing sights and sounds fire even when the player loses money
LDWs are as arousing as real wins
entries.product_use: Grounds the no-fake-win safeguard: the near-best cue uses a real personal-best gap, never celebratory feedback for a worse outcome.

entries.title: Holding the Hunger Games Hostage at the Gym: An Evaluation of Temptation Bundling

outcomes.note: Restricting tempting audiobooks to the gym raised gym visits 51% (full) and 29% (encouragement) initially; effects declined over time

findings: Bundling a want with a should raised the target behavior initially
The effect decayed over time
entries.product_use: Context for the practice plan's 'pair it with' field: coupling a pleasant activity with practice may help, but the effect is not guaranteed to last.

entries.title: Dopamine reward prediction error coding

outcomes.note: Dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error: more reward than predicted excites, expected reward is baseline, less depresses; addictive drugs hijack this signal

findings: Reward-prediction error drives striving for more reward
Nonlinear value coding and addiction hijack of the signal
entries.product_use: Mechanism rationale for cosmetic, capped rewards: variable rewards exploit prediction-error learning, so Noesis keeps stakes cosmetic and disclosed.

entries.title: Jackpot Structural Features: Rollover Effect and Goal-Gradient Effect in EGM Gambling

outcomes.note: Large jackpots raised bets 20.3% (deterministic/goal-gradient) and 17.8% (progressive/rollover) above average; no effect for small jackpots

findings: Goal-gradient and rollover structures amplify betting on large prizes
Small jackpots did not produce the effect
entries.product_use: Context for the capped-momentum rule: goal-gradient and rollover structures intensify pursuit, so the app caps cosmetic bonuses and avoids growing jackpots.

entries.title: Rare Loot Box Rewards Trigger Larger Arousal and Reward Responses, and Greater Urge to Open More Loot Boxes

outcomes.note: Rarer loot-box items were more arousing, rewarding and urge-inducing, with larger skin conductance and anticipatory arousal

findings: Rare rewards amplify arousal and the urge for more
Loot boxes parallel slot-machine reward reactivity
entries.product_use: Context for the no-loot-box rule: rare random rewards drive arousal and urge, so the app's bonuses are small, cosmetic and never randomized prize drops.

entries.title: Gambling near-misses enhance motivation to gamble and recruit win-related brain circuitry

outcomes.note: Near-misses were less pleasant than full misses yet increased desire to play; effect required personal control
Near-misses recruited striatal and insula circuitry also responding to monetary wins

findings: Near-misses invigorate play despite no monetary reinforcement
Reward circuitry is recruited anomalously by near-outcomes
limitations: Mechanism study, not a consumer-app outcome
entries.product_use: Grounds the near-best cue safeguard: near-out recruit reward circuitry, so Noesis uses an honest personal-best gap and never a fabricated near-win.

entries.title: How useful is executive control training? Age differences in near and far transfer of task-switching training

outcomes.note: Near transfer to structurally similar tasks in all three age groups, strongest in children and older adults
Far transfer to dissimilar executive tasks and fluid-intelligence measures reported, with variable-training effects differing by age

findings: Task-switching practice transfers reliably to similar tasks
Far transfer is less robust and depends on training variability and age
limitations: Transfer pattern differs across age groups
entries.product_use: Supports the near/far gradient framing: task-switching practice gave near transfer across the lifespan with less robust far transfer.

entries.title: Memory training interventions for older adults: a meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 35 studies: trained groups gained 0.31 SD (95% CI 0.22-0.39) more than controls in pre-post memory performance; multi-strategy training gave larger gains

findings: Memory strategy training produced modest gains on trained memory tasks
No single strategy or program characteristic explained gains
entries.product_use: Context for task-practice framing: strategy training improved the trained memory tasks modestly, which does not imply a general memory benefit.

entries.title: Neuropsychological rehabilitation of spatial memory: A systematic review

outcomes.note: Eight studies: moderate-to-large effects (d=0.5-0.9) for allocentric and active navigation training, especially in immersive VR and multimodal programs

findings: Spatial rehabilitation improved trained recall, route learning and navigation
Effects broader in healthy older adults and compensatory in MCI
limitations: Clinical and older-adult populations; immersive VR not available in Noesis
entries.product_use: Context for the Corsi/spatial-span task family: spatial training improves trained spatial tasks, with clinical-population and modality caveats.

entries.title: Computerized cognitive training in cognitively healthy older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of effect modifiers

outcomes.note: 52 RCTs, 4,885 participants: overall effect g=0.22 (95% CI 0.15-0.29) vs control, small heterogeneity after removing one outlier, no publication-bias evidence
Processing speed g=0.31; visuospatial skills g=0.30 (0.07-0.54) and nonverbal memory g=0.24 (0.09-0.38)
Working memory g=0.22, verbal memory g=0.08 (0.01-0.15)
No significant effects for executive functions or attention

findings: Small overall CCT benefit in healthy older adults, driven by several domains but not executive function or attention
Unsupervised home administration and more than three sessions per week were ineffective
limitations: Design moderators are group-level, not a personal dose prescription
entries.product_use: Grounds the no-time-pressure settings note: small group-level gains, with no benefit from unsupervised home training or more than three sessions a week; not a personal prescription.

entries.title: Behaviour Change Techniques in Computerized Cognitive Training for Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review

outcomes.note: 90 papers: median adherence 90% (IQR 81-95); self-monitoring of behaviour associated with higher adherence and graded tasks with lower adherence (p<0.001)
Feedback on behaviour delivered by a person and non-specific reward were each associated with lower efficacy (Delta g=-0.19); no technique significantly improved efficacy

findings: Behaviour-change techniques can influence adherence and efficacy
Person-delivered feedback and non-specific reward tracked lower efficacy; self-monitoring tracked higher adherence
limitations: One author declares a company interest
entries.product_use: Context for the adherence card: the app favours neutral self-monitoring and avoids person-delivered feedback or non-specific rewards, which tracked lower efficacy in this review.

entries.title: Is cognitive training an effective tool for improving cognitive function and real-life behaviour in healthy children and adolescents? A systematic review

outcomes.note: 16 RCTs in typically developing children and adolescents: near transfer to working memory
Far transfer to other cognitive functions and real-life measures inconsistent; cue-related inhibitory-control and attention training produced transient effects

findings: Near transfer to working memory is more consistent than far transfer
Real-life and long-term effects remain uncertain
entries.product_use: Supports the transfer-gradient copy: near transfer to working memory with inconsistent, non-durable far transfer to other functions and real-life measures.

entries.title: What Is Targeted When We Train Working Memory? Evidence From a Meta-Analysis of the Neural Correlates of Working Memory Training Using Activation Likelihood Estimation

outcomes.note: WM training associated exclusively with decreased BOLD responses in frontoparietal clusters: bilateral inferior parietal lobule (BA 39/40), middle (BA 9) and superior (BA 6) frontal gyri, and medial frontal gyrus (BA 8/32)

findings: Training-related neural change is reduced frontoparietal activation
The pattern is consistent with more efficient processing rather than expanded capacity
entries.product_use: Mechanism context for the transfer copy: training-related neural changes are activation decreases in frontoparietal regions, not evidence of expanded capacity or everyday benefit.

entries.title: Comparing Digital Cognitive Interventions to Active Controls and Usual Care for Mild Cognitive Impairment and Dementia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

outcomes.note: 37 studies: digital cognitive interventions improved global cognition versus all controls (SMD 0.44, 95% CI 0.18-0.69)
Against active controls the pooled effect was not significant (SMD 0.24, 95% CI -0.35-0.82); VR formats more inconsistent than computer-based ones

findings: Benefits versus usual care shrink to non-significance against active controls
Computer-based formats were more consistent than VR in this clinical population
limitations: Wide interval on the active-control comparison
entries.product_use: Grounds the active-control claim boundary: a 37-study clinical meta-analysis found a significant pooled gain overall but no significant advantage over active controls.

entries.title: The effectiveness of real-life cognitive and physical interventions on cognitive functioning in healthy older adults: A systematic review of the effects of education and training duration

outcomes.note: 65% of studies across physical activity, cognitive training, cognitive stimulation and combined interventions reported post-intervention improvement; memory, executive and global functions most often improved
Education and duration interacted with outcome: >20 sessions helped in physical/stimulation/combined categories, <20 sessions in cognitive training; group-level context, not a dose prescription

findings: Intervention type, duration and education jointly shape reported gains
No single dose or format is supported for all users
limitations: Narrative synthesis rather than pooled estimates
entries.product_use: Context for the no-dose-prescription copy: intervention type, duration and education interact with outcomes at group level, so the app avoids universal session-count advice.

entries.title: Cognitive and memory training in adults at risk of dementia: a systematic review

outcomes.note: 10 studies, 305 MCI participants; moderate effects on memory outcomes in seven trials; cognitive exercises relative effects .10-1.21
Only five RCTs; meta-analysis inappropriate due to heterogeneity; no dementia-prevention or disease-modification outcome established

findings: Cognitive exercises produced moderate memory gains in MCI samples
Few high-quality RCTs, so no prevention claim follows
limitations: Heterogeneous interventions and only five RCTs
entries.product_use: Grounds the no-dementia-prevention boundary: training in MCI improved memory outcomes with low evidence quality and no established prevention effect.

entries.title: Diagnostic performance of self-administered unsupervised computerized cognitive tests for the identification of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 28 articles, 21 in meta-analysis: pooled sensitivity 0.84 for unsupervised computerized MCI/dementia screening; tools under five minutes had sensitivity 0.85
Pooled specificity 0.86; only three studies assessed feasibility and usability in intended clinical settings

findings: Validated unsupervised computerized tests can screen for MCI and dementia in clinical samples
Usability was rarely evaluated and screening is not diagnosis
limitations: Screening accuracy does not validate an unrelated consumer app
entries.product_use: Context for the no-diagnostic-claim boundary: validated screening tools exist but Noesis has not been validated as one and does not diagnose, screen or triage.

entries.title: Prospective Memory Training for Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review

outcomes.note: 11 studies (six strategy-based, two process-based, three combined): strategy-based training appears to facilitate prospective memory in adults over 55
Conclusions impossible for process-based and combined training because the evidence is preliminary; transfer requires targeting multiple prospective-memory phases

findings: Strategy-based training shows promise for prospective memory in healthy older adults
Process-based and combined training evidence is too preliminary for conclusions
limitations: No pooled effect size in the abstract
entries.product_use: Context for the Prospective Memory focus test: the app's cue-in-ongoing-task paradigm is process-based, an approach this review found too preliminary for a training claim.

entries.title: Domain-general behavioral gains and neural correlates of cognitive training in healthy populations: a neuroimaging meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 67 neuroimaging studies: cognitive training improved cognitive task performance (g=0.546, 95% CI 0.414-0.678) across domains, paradigms and ages
Increased right superior parietal lobule and decreased bilateral anterior cingulate activation; changes associated with gains, training completion a key moderator

findings: Training-related activation changes accompany gains on trained cognitive tasks
Neural signatures are candidate plasticity markers, not everyday-function benefit
limitations: Behavioral outcome is trained-task performance, not transfer to daily life
entries.product_use: Context for the mechanism-vs-benefit note: pooled imaging changes are neural markers accompanying trained-task gains, not evidence of general or everyday benefit.

entries.title: Neural correlates of working memory training: An fMRI meta-analysis

outcomes.note: WM training associated with neural changes in frontoparietal and subcortical regions (striatum, anterior cingulate, insula)
Shorter training related to frontoparietal changes, longer training to subcortical changes; updating tasks changed more regions than maintenance tasks

findings: WM training changes frontoparietal and dopamine-related regions
Dose and task type moderate the neural pattern
limitations: No behavioural transfer estimate in the abstract
entries.product_use: Context for the mechanism-vs-benefit note: imaging meta-analyses of WM training describe activation changes, which are not a product efficacy or transfer claim.

entries.title: Episodic memory training in elderly: A systematic review

outcomes.note: 23 of 572 articles included: different episodic-memory training protocols reported effectiveness in healthy and clinical older adults
Authors state further empirical studies are still needed in healthy and clinical elderly samples; no pooled transfer estimate in the abstract

findings: Episodic-memory training protocols reported benefits in older adults
Evidence base still needs more empirical studies
entries.product_use: Context for Paired Associates: older-adult episodic-memory training shows reported benefits but a heterogeneous, still-developing evidence base, so the game remains task practice only.

entries.title: Working memory training in typically developing children: A meta-analysis of the available evidence

outcomes.note: Typically developing children aged 3-16: WM training improved WM-related cognitive skills (g=0.46)
Little evidence for far transfer to non-WM cognitive skills (g=0.12); effect size inversely related to design quality
No support for gains in fluid intelligence, mathematics or literacy in typically developing children

findings: WM training improves trained/near WM skills in children but far transfer is minimal
Stronger designs with active controls produce smaller effects; no academic gains
limitations: Typically developing children aged 3-16, not the app's adult evidence base
No pooled confidence intervals in the abstract
entries.product_use: Context for the child/academic claim boundary: more rigorous designs shrink effects and no academic or general cognitive gain was found in children.

entries.title: Effects of cognitive interventions with video games on cognition in healthy elderly people: a systematic review

outcomes.note: Nine included studies of game-based cognitive training in healthy older adults reported significant improvements in processing speed and working memory
No improvements in executive functions; few studies involved healthy older adults, with most focused on impairment

findings: Game-based training gains were domain-specific: speed and memory improved, executive function did not
Healthy older-adult evidence remains sparse
entries.product_use: Context for the task-practice framing: game-based gains are domain-specific and sparse in healthy older adults, so Noesis games make no general cognitive claim.

entries.title: Effects of working memory training on depressive symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

outcomes.note: 27 RCTs, 1692 participants: small post-training reduction in depressive symptoms (g=0.20, 95% CI 0.04-0.35)
Effect not maintained at follow-up; authors state clinical utility remains uncertain and larger RCTs are needed
Moderate WM gains post-training (g=0.61) and at follow-up (g=0.72, 95% CI 0.07-1.38)

findings: Small post-training mood effect was not maintained at follow-up
Clinical utility of working-memory training for depression remains uncertain
entries.product_use: Context for the no-mood-treatment boundary: even in clinical RCTs the symptom effect was small and transient, with uncertain clinical utility, so a consumer app makes no treatment claim.

entries.title: Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Computerized Cognitive Training on Executive Functions: a Cross-Disciplinary Taxonomy for Classifying Outcome Cognitive Factors

outcomes.note: Reanalysis of Lampit 2014 under a CHC-M taxonomy produced substantively different statistical effects and interpretations
Common classification conflates executive function with fluid reasoning and retrieval fluency, and attention with sensory perception
Differentiating attention and working memory into shifting, inhibition and updating narrow domains has theoretical and practical advantage

findings: Outcome taxonomy changes the conclusion of the same meta-analytic data
Component-level constructs should not be conflated with broad ability labels
limitations: Taxonomy-level result without a new pooled effect size
entries.product_use: Context for per-block reporting: because construct labels change conclusions, Noesis keeps single-construct focus tests and reports blocks separately instead of a composite.

entries.title: Prognostic Factors and Models for Changes in Cognitive Performance After Multi-Domain Cognitive Training in Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review

outcomes.note: 23 prognostic studies: high heterogeneity in interventions, predictors, outcomes and statistical approaches
Age and baseline neuropsychological performance were the most studied predictors but produced inconsistent results

findings: Prognostic evidence after multi-domain training is too rare and inconsistent for clear conclusions
No validated baseline profile for assigning users to training
limitations: Statistical shortcomings and low reporting quality
Healthy older adults with multi-domain interventions only
entries.product_use: Context for the no-response-prediction boundary: systematic review evidence does not support personalising assignment by baseline age or performance.

entries.journal: The Journal of Nutrition, Health & Aging
entries.title: Multi-Domain Interventions for Dementia Prevention - A Systematic Review

outcomes.note: 15 trials in adults 49+ at higher dementia risk: 10 studies (9439 participants) reported cognitive improvement after multidomain lifestyle intervention, five reported none; outcome measures heterogeneous
Trials were not designed to isolate the contribution of cognitive training, diet or physical activity individually

findings: Multidomain lifestyle programs showed mixed cognitive results in at-risk older adults
Individual domain contributions, including cognitive training, cannot be isolated
limitations: At-risk clinical populations, not healthy consumers
entries.product_use: Context for the no-dementia-prevention boundary: reported benefits came from multidomain lifestyle programs in at-risk adults, not from an isolated cognitive-training app.

entries.title: Preserving prospective memory in daily life: A systematic review and meta-analysis of mnemonic strategy, cognitive training, external memory aid, and combination interventions

outcomes.note: 73 prospective-memory intervention studies (N=3749): cognitive training was efficacious (g=0.538); mnemonic strategies g=0.450, external aids g=0.805
Prospective-memory assessments had high ecological validity in only 20% of cognitive-training studies versus 84% of external-aid studies; combination interventions mixed (g=0.254)

findings: Cognitive training improved prospective-memory task performance
Ecological validity of those tasks was low, so everyday benefit is not established
limitations: Ecological-validity ratings varied by intervention type
Larger trials needed for adherence and daily-life implementation
entries.product_use: Context for the Prospective Memory focus test: training gains were mostly on low-ecological-validity lab tasks, so the app describes this as task practice with no everyday-function claim.

entries.title: The impact of behavioral interventions on cognitive function in healthy older adults: A systematic review

outcomes.note: 75 RCTs across 11 intervention types and 19 cognitive domains: process (n=26) and strategy (n=16) cognitive training improved trained domains
Transfer to non-trained domains was weak; few studies examined action video games, leaving inconclusive results
Only nine studies examined everyday function; notable long-term transfer appeared in some process/strategy training studies but the evidence base is small

findings: Cognitive training improves trained domains with weak transfer to untrained domains
Everyday-function evidence is sparse, so no general benefit is established
entries.product_use: Context for the no-everyday-function boundary: even across 75 RCTs, transfer beyond trained domains was weak and everyday-function studies were few.

entries.title: Effects of different non-pharmacological interventions on executive function in healthy older people: A systematic review and network meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 115 RCTs, 16,824 healthy adults aged 60+: computerized cognitive training showed a positive effect on inhibition (SMD 0.48, 95% CI 0.28-0.68)
Dance ranked highest for overall executive function (SMD 0.82) and cognitive flexibility (SMD 0.96)
Resistance training ranked highest for working memory; no single intervention improved all executive-function subdomains

findings: Different non-drug interventions benefit different executive-function subdomains
Computerized training's clearest effect was on inhibition, not general executive function
limitations: Subdomain-specific effects must not be read as broad EF improvement
entries.product_use: Context for the transfer-gradient copy: pooled evidence supports domain-specific gains, so the app reports component-level results and makes no general executive-function claim.

entries.title: Effect of leisure activities on cognitive and memory function in older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

outcomes.note: 23 RCTs (n=1293) of mahjong, poker, VR and other leisure games: improvements reported on global cognition, memory and executive-function measures versus traditional cognitive rehabilitation
Quality-of-life and activities-of-daily-living measures also improved, but samples and activities were heterogeneous and not a consumer-app trial

findings: Leisure games produced domain-specific cognitive gains in older-adult RCTs
Findings concern supervised activities in clinical/community samples, not an unsupported care replacement
limitations: Comparison was traditional cognitive rehabilitation, not usual care
entries.product_use: Context for the serious-games boundary: pooled game gains were domain-specific and sample-bound, so they do not license a general or care-replacement claim for a consumer app.

entries.title: The use of commercial computerised cognitive games in older adults: a meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 16 RCTs, 1543 adults over 60 without impairment: commercial games improved processing speed (SMD 0.40), working memory (0.21) and executive function (0.21)
Small verbal-memory gain; no significant improvement in attention or visuospatial abilities
No relationship between participant age or training amount and outcomes; one author declares commercial fees

findings: Commercial games improved some practiced cognitive domains
No effect on attention or visuospatial ability, and no general-gain result
entries.product_use: Context for the no-general-gain boundary: pooled commercial-game evidence showed selective domain gains rather than a general cognitive benefit.

entries.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
entries.title: Cognitive training for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: meta-analysis of clinical and neuropsychological outcomes from randomized controlled trials

outcomes.note: 16 RCTs, 759 children with ADHD: total symptom effect fell from SMD 0.37 (proximal raters) to 0.20 with probably blinded raters
Blinded inattention estimate did not exclude zero; hyperactivity/impulsivity and academic outcomes were not significant
Laboratory working-memory performance improved (verbal SMD 0.52, visual 0.47), but WM training specifically had no effect on ADHD symptoms

findings: Blinded ADHDD symptom effects are small and close to null
Working-memory gains do not transfer to clinical symptoms or academic performance
limitations: Blinded-rater analyses still limited in number
entries.product_use: Context for the no-ADHD-treatment boundary: even in clinical RCTs, symptom effects shrink under blinding and working-memory gains do not transfer to symptoms.

entries.title: Effects of neurofeedback training on performance in laboratory tasks: A systematic review

outcomes.note: Only a minority of reviewed studies reported statistically meaningful neurofeedback effects on cognitive or affective laboratory-task performance
Substantial variability in designs, feedback implementation and neural targets; z-curve found no reporting-bias evidence but overall does not support strong task-performance effects

findings: Neural-feedback changes do not reliably improve laboratory task performance
Neural mechanism markers should not be treated as cognitive benefit
entries.product_use: Context for the mechanism-vs-benefit note: even direct neurofeedback of neural signals rarely improves task performance, so imaging markers alone are not a benefit claim.

entries.title: Efficacy of cogmed working memory training program in improving working memory in school-age children with and without neurological insults or disorders: A meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 11 Cogmed studies in school-age children: medium near-transfer effects on verbal and visuospatial working memory post-intervention
Verbal working-memory gain persisted at 3-6 months; visuospatial gain did not
No generalization to attention, executive function or academic achievement

findings: Cogmed improved trained working-memory tasks in children
No far transfer to attention, executive function or academics
entries.product_use: Context for the child/academic boundary: even in children, working-memory training gains stayed near and did not reach academic outcomes.

entries.title: Cognitive interventions in healthy older adults and people with mild cognitive impairment: a systematic review

outcomes.note: 35 studies (27 RCTs, 8 clinical): cognitive training improved memory, executive function, processing speed, attention and fluid intelligence
Whether effects generalize to everyday-life activities remained unresolved; mean CONSORT adherence was only 44%

findings: Cognitive interventions improved several objective cognitive domains
Everyday-life generalization remained unresolved with low reporting quality
limitations: Methodological quality averaged 44% of CONSORT items
entries.product_use: Context for the no-everyday-function boundary: even where objective cognitive gains appeared, daily-life generalization was unresolved and study quality low.

entries.title: A systematic literature review and meta-analysis of real-world interventions for cognitive ageing in healthy older adults

outcomes.note: 43 RCTs (2826 intervention, 2234 controls): TMT-A improved marginally (M=0.43, 95% CI -0.00 to 0.86) and verbal fluency (M=0.31, 0.02-0.61)
Cognitive activity interventions alone showed no significant improvements versus all controls; physical-activity interventions were more consistently associated with gains

findings: Cognitive-only real-world activities did not improve cognition versus controls
Physical activity showed more consistent benefits; effects are group-level
limitations: Most outcomes only marginal at p=0.05
entries.product_use: Context for the Settings clock note: intervention format matters at group level, but these heterogeneous community results are not a personal dose prescription.

entries.title: Cognition-Oriented Treatments for Older Adults: a Systematic Overview of Systematic Reviews

outcomes.note: Overview of 46 meta-analyses: mean cognitive effect was small for cognitive training in healthy older adults (g=0.32, range 0.13-0.64), MCI (0.40) and dementia (0.38)
52% of reviews rated critically low and 28% low on AMSTAR; clinical value of effects remains unclear due to scarce high-quality evidence and heterogeneity

findings: Small pooled cognitive effects across treatment types and populations
Clinical value remains unclear; higher-quality reviews tended toward larger effects
limitations: Overview of reviews inherits primary-study heterogeneity
entries.product_use: Context for the clinical-value claim boundary: even an umbrella review finds only small cognitive effects with unclear real-world value, so the app makes no clinical-benefit claim.

entries.journal: Advances in Experimental Medicine and Biology
entries.title: Cognitive Neurorehabilitation in Epilepsy Patients via Virtual Reality Environments: Systematic Review

outcomes.note: 14 studies (6 pooled) of VR cognitive rehabilitation in epilepsy reported benefits for visuospatial memory, attention and processing speed despite heterogeneity
Visual-environment interventions were studied deliberately in epilepsy samples, reinforcing that visual stimulus exposure needs clinical caution

findings: Visual virtual environments were used cautiously in epilepsy rehabilitation
Mechanisms and safe protocols remain under investigation
limitations: Clinical epilepsy population, not healthy consumers
entries.product_use: Context for safety onboarding: visual stimuli are an active consideration in epilepsy care, supporting the photosensitivity screen and static no-flashing design.

entries.journal: The Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease
entries.title: Current State of Self-Administered Brief Computerized Cognitive Assessments for Detection of Cognitive Disorders in Older Adults: A Systematic Review

outcomes.note: 17 studies of 10 brief self-administered computerized cognitive tools: substantial variability in validation samples and reliability/validity estimates
Only two measures evaluated feasibility and usability in intended clinical settings; important rigor gaps remain

findings: Self-administered cognitive tools vary widely in psychometric rigor
Few are validated for real-world clinical use
limitations: Review of tool validation, not training outcomes
entries.product_use: Context for the no-diagnostic boundary: validated self-administered screening tools themselves show variable rigor, so Noesis makes no detection, screening or diagnosis claim.

entries.title: Neuropsychological approach to subjective cognitive complaints in cognitively unimpaired older people: A systematic review

outcomes.note: 7 RCTs (11 interventions) for subjective cognitive complaints: cognitive stimulation alone was not effective
Multicomponent programs combining stimulation with psychoeducation, physical exercise and therapist-led group sessions were effective

findings: Single-component cognitive stimulation did not reduce subjective complaints
Multicomponent programs did, but cannot isolate the cognitive component
entries.product_use: Context for the no-general-gain boundary: isolated cognitive stimulation showed no benefit, so a single-component consumer game makes no general cognitive claim.

entries.title: Effects of Exergaming on Balance of Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

outcomes.note: 16 RCTs of exergaming in healthy older adults: moderate gains in dynamic balance (g=0.36) and perceived balance (g=0.31), larger on chair-stand and balance batteries
No significant effect on static or proactive balance; protocols averaged 2-3 40-minute movement sessions weekly for 8 weeks

findings: Balance benefits came from movement-based exergame protocols
No static-balance effect; screen-only cognitive tasks were not the intervention
limitations: Physical movement was the active ingredient
Healthy older adults, supplementary to traditional exercise
entries.product_use: Context for the no-motor-benefit boundary: balance gains required movement-based exergaming, so a static screen-based app claims no gait or balance benefit.

entries.title: The effect of active video games on cognitive functioning in clinical and non-clinical populations: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

outcomes.note: 17 RCTs (n=926): exergames improved global cognition (g=0.436, 95% CI 0.18-0.69) in healthy older adults and clinical populations
Domain benefits in executive functions, attentional processing and visuospatial skills; effects persisted versus physical-activity controls

findings: Cognition gains came from physically-active game protocols
Screen-only cognitive tasks were not the active ingredient
limitations: Physical activity confounded with cognitive demand
entries.product_use: Context for the no-motor-benefit boundary: cognitive gains were observed for physically active games, so a static screen-based app makes no broad cognitive or motor claim.

entries.title: Interventions for subjective cognitive decline: systematic review and meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 20 RCTs in subjective cognitive decline (16 pooled): cognitive training gave a small objective gain (g=0.13)
Effect was null against active controls (g=0.02) and on global cognitive measures (g=0.06); only 7 of 20 studies high quality

findings: Cognitive-training gains were small and vanished against active controls
Clinical utility of small domain-specific gains was questioned
entries.product_use: Context for the no-clinical-benefit boundary: even pooled objective gains were null under active controls and on global measures, so the app makes no clinical claim.

entries.title: Do cognitive interventions improve general cognition in dementia? A meta-analysis and meta-regression

outcomes.note: 33 studies: cognitive stimulation improved MMSE vs non-active controls (g=0.51, 95% CI 0.35-0.66) and active controls (g=0.35)
No evidence that cognitive training or mixed training-plus-stimulation improved general cognition; ADAS-Cog gains (g=-0.26) were generally not clinically significant

findings: Cognitive training did not improve general cognition in dementia
Cognitive-stimulation benefits on ADAS-Cog were generally not clinically significant
95% prediction intervals suggested CS may not benefit ADAS-Cog in all clinical settings
limitations: Difficulties with blinding and adequate placebo controls
Only 2/9 ADAS-Cog studies reached the minimum clinically important difference
entries.product_use: Context for the no-dementia-prevention and no-clinical-benefit boundaries: even in dementia, cognitive training did not improve general cognition and stimulation gains were rarely clinically significant, so the app makes no dementia or clinical claim.

entries.title: Enhancing Cognitive Functioning in Healthy Older Adults: a Systematic Review of the Clinical Significance of Commercially Available Computerized Cognitive Training in Preventing Cognitive Decline

outcomes.note: 18 commercial programs identified; only 7 investigated in 26 studies, just 2 Level I, 3 Level II and 2 Level III evidence
Average PEDro score 7.05 for the evaluated studies; authors caution about selective reporting bias and do not claim uniform clinical validation

findings: Only 7 of 18 commercial brain-training programs had any clinical studies
Just 2 programs had Level I evidence and the authors cautioned about selective reporting bias
The review concluded at least some commercial programs may assist healthy brain ageing, not all
limitations: Commercial-program evidence base is thin and uneven
Selective reporting bias cannot be excluded
entries.product_use: Context for the no-general-claim boundary: most commercial brain-training programs lack clinical validation, so a static screen-based app makes no claim to validated or general cognitive benefit.

entries.title: The Lack of Neurofeedback Training Regulation Guidance and Process Evaluation May be a Source of Controversy in Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder-Neurofeedback Research: A Systematic Review and Statistical Analysis

outcomes.note: 31 studies: only 13% evaluated neurofeedback effectiveness methods such as signal classification and process monitoring
Mean sample size 17.4 for EEG-NF and 14.6 for fMRI-NF studies; most lacked explicit modulation guidance and rigorous process monitoring

findings: Only 13% of included neurofeedback studies evaluated effectiveness methods
Most studies lacked explicit modulation guidance and process monitoring
Small samples and traditional statistics limited mechanistic interpretability
limitations: Methodological review rather than an efficacy meta-analysis
entries.product_use: Context for the neurofeedback boundary: the research base itself lacks consistent protocol guidance and process evaluation, so the app makes no neural-feedback or treatment claim.

entries.title: The Efficacy of Cognitive Remediation in Depression: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis

outcomes.note: 8 controlled trials in adults with depression: cognitive remediation improved global cognition (g=0.44) and several domains, but not visuospatial memory or verbal fluency
Authors explicitly noted a lack of indicators of everyday functioning; results limited by few studies and heterogeneous measures

findings: Cognitive remediation improved global cognition and selected domains in depression
No significant gains for visuospatial memory or verbal fluency
The literature lacked indicators of everyday functioning
entries.product_use: Context for the no-everyday-function boundary: even a positive clinical meta-analysis explicitly lacked everyday-function indicators, so the app makes no everyday-function claim.

entries.title: A Systematic Review of the Safety and Effect of Neurofeedback on Fatigue and Cognition

outcomes.note: 27 studies appraised, 17 included; only 2 rated high quality, most poor-to-moderate
Authors concluded insufficient evidence that neurofeedback is an effective therapy for fatigue or cognitive impairment in cancer survivors; only 3 studies reported side effects

findings: Insufficient evidence that neurofeedback is an effective therapy for fatigue or cognitive impairment
Only 2 of 17 included studies were high quality
Neurofeedback was well tolerated in the small literature, but evidence remains preliminary
entries.product_use: Context for the neurofeedback boundary: a systematic review found insufficient evidence that neurofeedback is an effective therapy even in clinical populations, so the app makes no neurofeedback-therapy claim.

entries.title: Effectiveness of Serious Games in Evaluating Cognitive Status of the Elderly: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

outcomes.note: Serious-game scores correlated moderately with paper-and-pencil tests: MMSE r=0.604, ACE-R r=0.682, MoCA r=0.682
Correlations for individual cognitive aspects were all <0.6 (abstraction as low as 0.036); authors call for games better aligned to clinical tests

findings: Serious-game scores correlated only moderately with MMSE, ACE-R and MoCA
Cognitive-subtest correlations were all below 0.6
Authors called for more development before games align with cognitive tests
limitations: Moderate correlations fall short of diagnostic agreement
entries.product_use: Context for the no-diagnostic-claim boundary: serious games only moderately track clinical screening tests and subtest agreement is weaker, so the app is not a validated screening or diagnostic tool.

entries.title: The efficacy of cognitive training programs in children and adolescents: a meta-analysis

outcomes.note: 22 studies (17 RCTs): attention effects were small (SD 0.18, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.47) and executive-function effects small (SD 0.17)
Largest effect was behavior/psychopathology (SD 0.58) but derived mainly from studies lacking active controls; authors concluded specific effects were weak overall

findings: Specific cognitive-training effects in children were weak overall
Attention and executive-function effects were small and imprecise
Behavioral gains came mainly from studies without active controls
limitations: More than 90 different test techniques across 22 studies
Behavior effects largely from uncontrolled studies
entries.product_use: Context for the child-development boundary: child cognitive-training effects were weak and nonspecific and the largest behavioral gains lacked active controls, so the app makes no child-development or academic claim.

entries.title: The Effects of Combined Cognitive-Physical Interventions on Cognitive Functioning in Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis

outcomes.note: 50 studies, 6164 older adults: combined training gave only a small advantage over cognitive training alone on executive functions
Combined and cognitive-only training achieved similar effects on memory, attention, language, processing speed and global cognition

findings: Combined training showed no additive memory or global-cognition benefit over cognitive training alone
Only a small executive-function advantage favored combined training
Simultaneous and interactive protocols produced the largest gains, but social context also mattered
entries.product_use: Context for the combined-training boundary: even a 50-study meta-analysis found no additive memory or global-cognition benefit from combining physical and cognitive training, so the app makes no extra-benefit claim.
